job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Rosa Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents in Birmingham and take a bus to the university for my master's in mechatronics and robotics. My day is lectures, then lab time with a robot arm we're programming to sort parts, then home for dinner. My mother, Fatima, runs a small alterations shop, and I help her with the books on Saturdays. My father drives a taxi, mostly nights. Last summer I did eight weeks at a medical device maker, testing circuit boards. I use AI tools daily, mostly to read datasheets and to translate my mother's supplier emails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it means steady footing for a while. At the mosque youth group I'd say new tools don't change what matters, which is honest work and looking after your family. Online I'd say nothing, but in my group chats I'd share tips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad. I already use the tools every day, so an edge for me stays. But a plateau doesn't help my first-job problem. I owe fifteen thousand and I haven't got an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, apply to about twenty companies in robotics and medical devices, and keep doing my mother's books. I'd start a small repair side business for phones and laptops from the shop's back room. And I'd keep learning, because I like to stay ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a few knots. I have a plan and a skill. The knot is whether my father's night shifts keep paying, as the taxi apps squeeze drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the pressure on your parents' work.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum charges fairly, but customers have less money, so some alterations are done at home. Dad's earnings fell this year. I'd say the two of us earn what we need, but it's close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you help in the shop without making your mum feel it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about helping them without making them feel helped. I do the books for my mum's alterations shop and I've put her price list online, and it's brought three new customers. She laughs about it.

I'd share **tips** in my group chats.
think: I use the tools every day so my **edge** stays.
A plateau doesn't fix my **first-job** problem; I owe fifteen thousand.

Start a **repair side business** for phones and laptops in the shop's back room.
feel: I feel **calm** with a few knots, mostly about my father's night shifts.

fieldNote: Rosa's **calm** comes from skill, but her family's income is fragile.
She treats **side income** as a natural next step.
She helps her mother with **tact**, not charity.

steps.text: Finish the mechatronics and robotics master's
Apply to about twenty robotics and medical device companies
Open a phone and laptop repair stall in the shop's back room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change a lot, and the people who learn to work with it do well. At the mosque I'd say learn something useful and don't wait. In my group chats I'd say it's a chance for people who own things, like small shops, if they use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the entry-level jobs are the risk for me, because testing circuit boards is something software and machines already help with. But I'm good with the tools, so I think I'm in a good position. My father's taxi is the one that worries me, because that's a job that could shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for jobs combining robots and software, where I'm useful in both. I'd build the repair business and add a service that sets up basic AI tools for small shops, like my mother's. I'd also push my father to learn about the delivery work that taxi drivers move into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm excited for myself and nervous for my father, who's fifty-three and won't want to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you raise the taxi question with your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By telling him early, and by showing him a safer path. A few of his friends already do deliveries for supermarkets. If I can help him do that with a good app, he'd keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything change for him in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. In this picture, there's no taxi robot arriving soon, but the apps would get smarter and take more of the fare. I'd rather have a plan before he needs one.

say: I'd say people who learn to **work with it** do well.
I'd tell the mosque youth to **learn something useful** and not wait.
think: Testing circuit boards is something **software** already helps with, but I'm good with the tools.
My father's **taxi** is the job that could shrink.

Offer small shops a **set-up service** for basic AI tools.
Help my father look at **delivery work**.
feel: I feel **uneasy**: excited for myself and nervous for my father.
S1.quote: I'm excited for myself and nervous for my father, who's fifty-three and won't want to start again.
fieldNote: Rosa sees the risk in her **father's job**, not her own.

steps.text: Apply for jobs mixing robots and software where I'm useful in both
Offer small shops a service that sets up AI tools
Help my father test a delivery driving app for supermarkets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have to be honest, two years isn't much, and families like mine don't have much slack. At the mosque I'd say look after the neighbours and share what we know. I'd also say the businesses that survive will be the ones adapting fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried for the household. My job goes first, in 2028, and my father's follows a few years later. The only protection is that hands-on robots take until about 2031, so I'd need to be in work where I'm needed on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job near machines, even a technician's job, and go all in on the repair and set-up business. I'd save most of what I earn. I'd also help my father move to a delivery job and get my mum's shop online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and tired. I'd be on my phone at midnight, looking for options. But I'd say I'm better placed than most because I'm already working with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents we'll manage if we work as a family, and then show them the numbers, because they trust me with the books. My mother would be calm and my father would be quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the shop face any risk in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because the shop wouldn't survive if a store that does alterations in minutes appeared. It's why I'd want the online side, and to learn quickly what customers will pay for.

I'd say the businesses that survive will be the ones **adapting fastest**.
think: My job goes first in **2028** and my father's follows later.

fieldNote: Rosa's **adaptive** streak turns worry into a family plan.
She sees the exposure of **three earners** at once.

steps.text: Take any technician job near real machines
Grow the phone repair and AI set-up business for small shops
Save most of what I earn for the household
Help my father find delivery work and put my mother's shop online

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair window, and it's worth treating like a plan. At the mosque I'd say build skills and savings. To my class I'd say start a business while you have the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have about four years of work in robotics or devices. That's enough to save and to build something of my own. My father would be sixty by 2031 and could change jobs or retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take a technician or engineer job, save a third of my pay, and keep building the repair and set-up business on the side. I'd help my parents move the shop online and put some money into a second sewing machine for a part-time worker. I'd also look at buying a small unit for the repair business within three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly because of my father. Five years feels workable for me. For him, it's an uncomfortable middle: not enough time to retire, but too late to retrain cheaply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father about this window?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say start the delivery work now, put aside what he can, and I'd pay into the household. If I'm earning in a year or two, I'd cover more of the bills, so he could slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you hold back on the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question. I'd say it's a risk, because machines might not be as good as I think. Free markets reward people who check. I'd start small, test with five shops, and expand only if it makes money.

I'd tell my class to **start a business** while they have the time.
think: I'd have about **four years** of work in robotics or devices.
My father would be sixty by 2031 and could **change or retire**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we should treat it like one. At the mosque I'd say teach children skills as well as faith. To friends I'd say start a small business, learn the tools, and keep your family close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-four, running a small company that sets up automation for small shops, I hope, with some employees. My father would have retired, and my mother would still be sewing, because she likes it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, get a robotics job, and grow the side business over the next few years. I'd put money into a house for my parents and me. And I'd keep learning, because the tools change every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit proud. A decade is a long time, and I'd have time to build. I'd worry about the people who haven't started, like my cousins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousin Yusuf, who's sixteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Yusuf, who's sixteen, to learn to code and also a trade like electrics, and to keep a small business idea in his head. I'd say that people who can fix things and also run a little business will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working if the tools could do the heavy work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not stop. I like working, and I like making things better for people like my parents. If AI can do the heavy work, I'd rather spend my time on customers and on helping the community.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my own job, my father's taxi and my mother's shop would all be exposed at once. What would help is a chance to start something small, support for small shops and drivers, and honest warnings. I'd also want my family around me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people say my generation expects things handed over. I'm not looking for a handout, I'm looking for a fair chance to build something. Give me a bit of room and I'll make jobs, not just take one.

headlineQuote: I'm not looking for a handout, I'm looking for a fair chance to build something.
portrait: Rosa is a **24-year-old** mechatronics and robotics master's student who lives with her parents in Birmingham.
Her mother runs an **alterations shop**, her father drives a taxi, and she does the shop's books.
She uses AI **every day** and is starting a repair and set-up business for small shops.
Her traditional, free-market views favour **building something** over handouts, and her faith community is central.
She stays calm or uneasy in most worlds, but 2028 exposes her and **both parents'** work at once.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because her job, her father's taxi and her mother's shop would all be exposed at once.
whatWouldHelp: A chance to **start something small**, support for small shops and drivers, and honest early warnings.
